blindSummary:
This state/province adopted a state/province-level declaration declaring itself free of LGBT ideology in 2020, repealed on 20 September 2021 under funding pressure from a supranational body, placing it in the same five-unit configuration as more conservative neighbouring state/provinces. The regional declaration carried the same intent as its neighbouring states/provinces: to exclude a visible public LGBTQ presence from the state/province’s civic space.

Within the same unit, however, its capital city — the country’s second city — has moved decisively the other direction. In May 2024 the newly elected mayor announced he would become the first mayor of the city ever to attend the city’s LGBT equality march and would fly a rainbow flag at city hall. His predecessor (in office 2002–2024) had only become an honorary patron of the march in 2021 and never attended. For a visitor in the old town, the operative institutional signal is the mayor’s public presence, not the repealed regional document.

Local risk sits above the country-wide average — the resolution history pulls it down, the capital city’s positive trajectory prevents a deeper drop. It is safer than two conservative neighbouring state/provinces — one without any equivalent large-city counter-signal, one whose capital actively banned a march — but less safe than the neighbouring state/province containing the national capital, whose institutional machinery works continuously in the visitor’s favour.
